newsitem.title: USA: CBOT says screen may help price muni index.
newsitem.headline: CBOT says screen may help price muni index.

text.p: A proposed electronic system for displaying bids and asks for bonds in the Bond Buyer municipal bond index may be used to help price the index, a Chicago Board of Trade official said on Wednesday.
Steve Sural, director of the CBOT's financial markets group, said the system could be used to supplement or enhance broker pricing of the 40 bonds in the index.
Sural, who was speaking at the exchange's annual municipal bond forum in Chicago, said he did not, however, envision eliminating the six pricing brokers that currently price the index.
The CBOT used the forum to open discussion about changes it proposes to make in the index aimed at sparking increased use of the futures contract.

The electronic screen system was by far the most radical change under consideration. While the system has been discussed in the past without much success, CBOT officials said this time the exchange itself would be facilitating the creation of the system, with or without vendor participation.
"The board of trade will aid that development," Sural said. "We feed the addition of a live trading screen will really increase price transparency."

Other changes proposed were increasing the minimum size of bond issues in the index to $75 million from $50 million, expanding the evaluation time for determining whether or not to delete bonds from the index due to illiquidity to 20 days from the current 10 days and allowing deleted bonds to return to the index as long as they continue to meet index criteria.
A new proposal was also announced that would raise the minimum trade size on which a pricing broker prices a bond issue to $1 million from $100,000.

While the exchange is hoping to nudge up sluggish open interest that has lately stood at 8,800 contracts by enticing more institutional use of the contract, one mutual fund manager attending the meeting said the minor "tweeks" in the contract would not increase the contract's appeal. He said his fund generally uses the U.S. Treasury bond futures contract instead of the municipal bond contract.

Sural said the proposals have been met with positive feedback from floor traders. If the feedback from traders and other contract users continues to be positive, the proposals would be put up for approval by the exchange. If approved, they would be sent to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission for its stamp of approval.
He predicted the changes could be in place as soon as the end of the year or early next year.
